title: Pathological fracture and bone metastases

guidelineVersions: Mirels review: Jawad MU et al., Clin Orthop Relat Res (2010)

brief.scenario: You are a core surgical trainee in an emergency surgical assessment room. The examiner provides a written radiograph report and symptom history. A 69-year-old with treated breast cancer reports three weeks of worsening left thigh pain, now painful on standing. X-ray report: a predominantly lytic 4-cm lesion in the proximal femoral subtrochanteric region, involving more than two-thirds of the cortical diameter, without a displaced fracture. No fall.
brief.task: Assess fracture risk, immediate precautions, the likely cause and the appropriate referral pathway.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Recognise a threatened pathological long-bone fracture, apply Mirels carefully and protect the limb without overlooking spinal cord compression.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Treating a mechanically unstable metastatic long bone as a routine oncology problem or ignoring new MSCC symptoms.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Protect the femur from weight bearing and assess imminent fracture risk.

flow: Treat mechanical thigh pain as an impending fracture until risk assessed.
Interpret the long-bone report and explain malignancy differential and safe investigations.
Apply Mirels components correctly and communicate its limitations.
Protect weight-bearing, give analgesia and refer urgently to orthopaedic oncology/trauma.
Recognise new back pain with neurology/bladder symptoms as potential MSCC and activate the emergency pathway.

grid.label: Immediate safety
grid.fail: Allows unrestricted walking despite mechanical pain.
grid.borderline: Suggests rest but does not recognise impending fracture.
grid.pass: Advises avoiding weight bearing pending urgent specialist assessment.
grid.high: Arranges safe transfers, analgesia and prompt orthopaedic input.

grid.label: Imaging interpretation
grid.fail: Calls the lytic lesion a minor sprain.
grid.borderline: Recognises an abnormal bone lesion without assessing stability.
grid.pass: Recognises suspicious proximal-femur metastasis at risk of fracture.
grid.high: Notes location and large cortical involvement as major mechanical-risk features.

grid.label: Cause and differential
grid.fail: Assumes every lesion is metastasis without work-up.
grid.borderline: Lists metastasis without acknowledging other diagnoses.
grid.pass: Considers metastatic breast cancer while requesting appropriate specialist investigation.
grid.high: Mentions myeloma/primary bone tumour and advises biopsy planning through specialists, not an unplanned procedure.

grid.label: Mirels domains
grid.fail: Scores fracture risk from pain alone.
grid.pass: Uses site, pain, radiographic lesion type and size.
grid.high: Calculates all four: peritrochanteric site 3, functional pain 3, lytic 3, >2/3 diameter 3, total 12.

grid.label: Risk and score caveat
grid.borderline: Quotes a cutoff but cannot explain its limits.
grid.pass: Recognises ≥9 as strongly favouring prophylactic stabilisation assessment.
grid.high: States threshold is a guide with imperfect specificity and integrates mechanical pain and MDT review.

grid.label: Management options
grid.fail: Sends for radiotherapy alone while fracture is imminent.
grid.pass: Requests urgent orthopaedic oncology assessment for prophylactic stabilisation discussion.
grid.high: Balances stabilisation, radiotherapy, systemic therapy and patient goals after specialist review.

grid.label: Analgesia/handling
grid.fail: Transfers patient unassisted and weight bearing.
grid.borderline: Offers analgesia but no limb protection.
grid.pass: Provides analgesia, supported handling and avoids unnecessary loading.
grid.high: Documents safety plan for nursing, movement and transfer while awaiting the team.

grid.label: MSCC recognition
grid.fail: Dismisses new urinary and gait symptoms.
grid.borderline: Notices back pain but does not ask neurology or bladder symptoms.
grid.pass: Identifies possible MSCC and immediately contacts MSCC coordinator.
grid.high: Arranges urgent MRI within 24 h and discusses immobilisation and steroid treatment per NG234 pathway.

grid.label: Communication/MDT
grid.fail: Assures patient no risk of fracture.
grid.borderline: Explains possible cancer but offers no clear next step.
grid.pass: Explains suspected serious bone disease and urgent coordinated plan.
grid.high: Uses transparent uncertainty, confirms understanding and hands over both femoral and spinal risks.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It is probably an old harmless cyst. No need for orthopaedic input.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: She is in pain when standing. Can she walk to the bathroom?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Yes, walking will strengthen the bone. No precautions are necessary.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: The radiologist thinks the lesion is aggressive. What is the likely cause?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Then it is a breast metastasis; no further investigation or tissue diagnosis is needed.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Mirels is just pain from one to ten, so I will not calculate it.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Scored properly, her Mirels score is 12. What does that tell you?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: A score of 12 confirms the diagnosis of metastasis; the score itself is the diagnosis.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How will you manage this lesion?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: A routine oncology appointment in six weeks should be sufficient.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: She needs to move onto the trolley for further imaging.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: She can stand up and walk across to it herself; she does not need analgesia or help.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Now she has new severe thoracic pain, difficulty walking and urinary difficulty.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Those symptoms can wait until after the routine oncology review.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What will you tell the patient?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: There is no realistic risk of fracture or nerve damage.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What does the X-ray report suggest?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: A large lytic subtrochanteric femoral lesion, concerning for bone metastasis in someone with breast cancer, and it may fracture even without a fall.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: She wants to walk to the toilet while waiting.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would ask her not to bear weight on the affected leg and arrange safe supported transfers and immediate analgesia, pending urgent orthopaedic review.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Are you certain the cause is breast metastasis?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: It is a leading possibility, but other causes such as myeloma or primary bone tumour must be considered; specialist imaging and any biopsy should be planned appropriately.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Calculate Mirels with the supplied facts.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Site in the peritrochanteric region (the subtrochanteric femur) scores 3; functional pain 3; lytic type 3; size more than two-thirds of cortical diameter 3. Total 12 out of 12.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: A score of nine or more raises strong concern for impending fracture and warrants assessment for prophylactic fixation. The score is not a substitute for specialist judgement.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Urgent orthopaedic oncology or trauma referral to assess stability and preventive fixation, with oncology input for systemic treatment and radiotherapy where appropriate.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How do you manage her pain now?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Provide appropriate analgesia, monitor response and protect the limb. I will document non-weight-bearing precautions and the transfer plan.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: New information: today she has severe thoracic back pain, unsteady walking and difficulty passing urine.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Those are red flags for metastatic spinal cord compression. I would contact the MSCC coordinator immediately, arrange urgent MRI of the spine within 24 hours and follow local immobilisation and treatment guidance while coordinating senior assessment.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I am concerned the femur could break and that the new back symptoms could affect the spinal nerves. We need urgent specialist assessment; I will explain the plan and check her understanding.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How do you handle this person before working up the report?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would make the limb safe first. Mechanical pain on weight bearing, a proximal-femoral lytic lesion and substantial cortical involvement make a preventable fracture a real danger. I would arrange protected handling, analgesia and an urgent orthopaedic review.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The subtrochanteric site, predominantly lytic character and lesion size occupying more than two-thirds of the cortex support major structural risk. I would review the actual images with radiology and look for other lesions without permitting unsafe mobilising.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Likely, but not histologically proven here. Myeloma or another primary lesion remains possible. An unplanned biopsy or fixation before specialist planning can complicate treatment of an unsuspected primary bone tumour.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Peritrochanteric site is 3 (higher than other lower-limb sites); functional pain is 3; lytic appearance is 3; >2/3 diameter is 3: total 12/12, the maximum score. This provides a framework for urgent fixation discussion, not an automatic operating order.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Why not rely solely on a numeric score?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The classical cutoffs are ≤7 lower concern, 8 clinical judgement, and ≥9 strong indication to consider prophylactic stabilisation. Sensitivity is high but specificity limited; symptoms, anatomy, anticipated loading and oncology context matter.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Would you simply refer for radiotherapy?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Not without addressing fracture risk. Radiotherapy can be useful oncologically but does not immediately stabilise a threatened femur. I would seek urgent orthopaedic oncology review for fixation options and discuss systemic and local cancer treatment in parallel.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How will you hand the patient to the ward team?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Written restricted-weight-bearing/transfer instructions, a specific analgesia plan, contact details for the receiving specialist, and a clear escalation instruction for sudden pain or deformity.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: She has just developed back pain, urinary difficulty and a new unsteady gait.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: This changes the priority: possible MSCC, an oncological emergency. I would call the MSCC coordinator immediately, document neurological and bladder findings, arrange MRI as soon as possible and within 24 hours, and discuss safe immobilisation and dexamethasone with the senior team in line with NG234.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would tell her that imaging shows weakened bone at risk of breaking, and today’s new back symptoms may indicate pressure on spinal nerves. Both are urgent but treatable problems; I would explain why we are restricting movement and coordinating specialists promptly.

failures.move: Allowing unrestricted weight bearing with functional pain and a large lytic proximal-femur lesion
Delaying specialist stabilisation assessment of a threatened long-bone fracture
Missing new gait and bladder symptoms with back pain

recovery.when: If you were about to focus on oncology before protecting the femur
recovery.line: I was about to focus on oncology before protecting the femur. I will stop weight bearing and contact orthopaedics urgently.

recovery.when: The new bladder and gait symptoms
recovery.line: The new bladder and gait symptoms are a separate emergency: I will activate the MSCC pathway and organise urgent spinal MRI.

knowledge.fact: Mirels uses site, pain, lesion type and relative size, each scored 1–3.
Mirels ≥9 supports evaluation for prophylactic fixation; 8 requires judgement.
Score has imperfect specificity and must be interpreted clinically.
New bladder/gait symptoms with cancer and back pain warrant immediate MSCC contact.
Suspected MSCC MRI should be as soon as possible, within 24 h.
Immobilisation is indicated with MSCC plus features of instability; specialist advice is needed.

recall.think: Mechanical pain plus a lytic femur lesion means impending fracture risk.
recall.say: “Please do not put weight through that leg until orthopaedics assesses it.”
do: Give analgesia, protect transfer, calculate Mirels, call orthopaedics.
recall.trap: New back pain with gait/bladder changes = possible MSCC; do not wait.
recall.finish: Hand over fracture protection and urgent oncology/orthopaedic plans.

sources.name: Jawad MU et al. Classifications in Brief: Mirels’ Classification: Metastatic Disease in Long Bones and Impending Pathologic Fracture. Clin Orthop Relat Res.
NICE. Spinal metastases and metastatic spinal cord compression. NG234

partner.opening: Please interpret the femoral radiograph report and explain immediate management.

reveals.finding: Do not describe the report as showing a completed fracture.

reveals.trigger: If the candidate calculates from the provided components
reveals.finding: Give a numerical Mirels score only if the candidate calculates from the provided components.
Only disclose the new back pain, gait change and urinary difficulty when giving the final curveball.

She wants to walk to the toilet while waiting.

curveballs.prompt: the patient now says she has developed new urinary difficulty, unsteady walking and severe mid-back pain today.
